sql_schemas: table leave_requests | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, start_date, end_date, requested_days, reason, status, approver_id, approval_comment, submitted_at, decided_at, cancelled_by, cancelled_at, reverses_request_id | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code; approver_id -> employees.id; cancelled_by -> employees.id; reverses_request_id -> leave_requests.id | indexes: reverses_request_id: UNIQUE (partial, non-null only) — a completed approval may be reversed at most once, so this index is what structurally guarantees the balance release happens exactly once; it also serves the lookup that detects an already-reversed original before a second release is attempted; reverses_request_id: also the access path for 'find the reversal of this request' when rendering the two-row wire representation; (employee_id, status): existing composite — role-scoped list queries (employeeIds = ANY(...)) combined with the status filter; status: status-filtered queries and lifecycle lookups (e.g. finding the APPROVED original); (leave_type_code, start_date): existing composite — leave-type + date-range filtering and the start_date DESC ordering of GET /leaves; employee_id: single-employee lookups and the leading column of the composite above

table leave_balances | fields: id, employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end, entitled_days, used_days, pending_days | pk: id | fks: employee_id -> employees.id; leave_type_code -> leave_types.code | indexes: (employee_id, leave_type_code, period_start, period_end): UNIQUE — findByKey resolves exactly one balance row for the accrual period containing the request's start_date; the uniqueness is the invariant the release arithmetic depends on; employee_id: current-balance reads for one employee (GET /balances/me) and the leading column of the unique key

table audit_logs | fields: id, actor_id, action, entity_type, entity_id, before_state, after_state, occurred_at | pk: id | fks: actor_id -> employees.id (logical reference; the initial migration stores it as an unconstrained string) | indexes: (entity_type, entity_id): existing composite — reconstruct the audit trail for one leave request; the reversal writes its CANCEL entry against the NEW row's id, so the trail of the original stays untouched; actor_id: 'what did this actor do' queries and the leading column for actor-scoped audit review

table notifications | fields: id, recipient_id, type, title, message, related_entity_type, related_entity_id, status, created_at, read_at | pk: id | fks: recipient_id -> employees.id | indexes: (recipient_id, status): existing composite — an employee's unread/read notification list; (related_entity_type, related_entity_id): locate the notifications attached to a given leave request; the cancellation notification points at the reversal row's id, not the immutable original

table employees | fields: id, employee_number, first_name, last_name, email, password_hash, role, manager_id, department, hire_date, termination_date, employment_status | pk: id | fks: manager_id -> employees.id | indexes: email: UNIQUE — login lookup and duplicate-email rejection; employee_number: UNIQUE — natural-key lookup and duplicate rejection; manager_id: direct-report resolution for MANAGER role scoping and the direct-manager cancellation authorization check

table leave_types | fields: code, name, requires_approval, max_consecutive_days, is_paid | pk: code | indexes: code: primary key / natural key — the FK target for leave_requests.leave_type_code and leave_balances.leave_type_code; static catalog, no lifecycle-driven index needed

data_notes:
PERSISTENCE SLICE — GP-008 reversal.

Schema delta (one knex migration, `migrations/<ts>_add_reverses_request_id_to_leave_requests.js`): add nullable `reverses_request_id` to `leave_requests` (self-referencing FK to `leave_requests.id`), plus a UNIQUE index on `reverses_request_id` restricted to non-null values. `up` adds column + index; `down` drops both. No other table changes. `leave_requests` is defined exactly once (see the saved spec) and referenced by name everywhere else.

Why the unique index is the load-bearing artifact: the acceptance criterion "returned exactly once, in the same transaction" is enforced structurally, not by application discipline. A second reversal of the same original cannot insert a second row, so the balance release cannot run twice. The service additionally calls `findByReversesRequestId` before releasing and throws ConflictError(409) if a reversal already exists, so the common case fails with a clean 409 rather than a raw unique-violation.

Model / DTO changes (persistence contract, not DDL):
- `LeaveRequest` gains `reversesRequestId: string | null` (15th field). `CreateLeaveRequestInput = Omit<LeaveRequest,'id'>` therefore carries it; `create` supplies `null` for every non-reversal row.
- `UpdateLeaveRequestDto` deliberately does NOT gain `reversesRequestId` and `FIELD_COLUMNS` does NOT gain it: the column is write-once at insert. This is what makes the original APPROVED row immutable — `update` has no path that can touch `reverses_request_id`, and the reversal path never calls `update` on the original at all.
- `PgLeaveRequestRepository`: `COLUMNS`, `LeaveRequestRow`, `mapRow` and the `create` INSERT all gain `reverses_request_id`; new `findByReversesRequestId`.
- Read model: `reversesRequestId` is returned by `findById`/`findByQuery`, so `GET /leaves` and `GET /leaves/:id` expose it and a client can tell the immutable APPROVED original (null) from the CANCELLED reversal (points at the original).

Write paths by state (unchanged for DRAFT/SUBMITTED):
- DRAFT / SUBMITTED cancel: `repository.update(id, {status: CANCELLED, cancelledBy, cancelledAt})` in place — no completed approval exists, GP-008 does not apply. SUBMITTED additionally releases `pendingDays -= requestedDays`.
- APPROVED cancel: the original row is NEVER updated. `repository.create({...original fields, status: CANCELLED, cancelledBy, cancelledAt, reversesRequestId: original.id, approverId: null, approvalComment: null, decidedAt: null})` inserts the reversal; `balanceRepository.update(balance.id, {usedDays: balance.usedDays - requestedDays})` releases the full count once. The original's status/approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt are byte-identical before and after.
- Audit: one CANCEL entry per cancellation, `entityId` = the reversal row's id, `beforeState` = the original APPROVED row, `afterState` = the reversal row — so the audit trail of the original is not rewritten.
- Notification: unchanged, `relatedEntityId` = the reversal row's id.

Balance read: `findByKey(..., forUpdate = true)` before the release, exactly as submit/approve/reject, so concurrent decisions cannot compute from a stale `usedDays`.

Acceptance mapping: the required test asserts (a) the original row still reads APPROVED with unchanged approverId/approvalComment/decidedAt, (b) a new CANCELLED row exists whose `reversesRequestId` equals the original id, (c) `usedDays` decreased by exactly `requestedDays` once, (d) one CANCEL audit row. `npm run smoke` must seed/assert the two-row representation via `GET /leaves`.

open_questions.question: Is a reversal row (status CANCELLED, reverses_request_id set) itself terminal, or may it be cancelled/reversed again — and if so, does the balance release apply a second time?
open_questions.impact: Determines whether the release-exactly-once guarantee needs a chain-depth guard beyond the unique index on reverses_request_id, and whether the cancellation authorization/timing guards must reject a request whose status is CANCELLED. If reversals are re-cancellable, the unique index alone no longer bounds the number of releases.
candidate_options: Reversal rows are terminal: cancel() rejects any request whose status is CANCELLED with ConflictError(409); the unique index on reverses_request_id is the complete exactly-once guarantee
Chained reversals allowed: each reversal may itself be reversed, requiring a depth/cycle guard and a per-row release ledger rather than a single unique index

open_questions.question: Should the NEW reversal row copy the original's approver_id, approval_comment and decided_at for provenance, or leave them null because the reversal itself was never approved?
open_questions.impact: Affects the read model a client sees for the CANCELLED row and whether the audit afterState of the reversal carries the original decision metadata. Copying them makes the reversal row look like it was approved (it was not); leaving them null loses the decision provenance that the immutable original still holds.
candidate_options: Leave approver_id/approval_comment/decided_at null on the reversal row — the original row remains the sole record of the approval, reachable via reverses_request_id
Copy the original's approver_id/approval_comment/decided_at onto the reversal row as a denormalized provenance snapshot

transaction_contract:
The APPROVED reversal is a multi-step atomic write (insert reversal row + release balance + audit + notification), so the contract is REQUIRED and is the existing service-owned unit of work, unchanged in shape.

- Repository methods that must join a caller's transaction take an OPTIONAL trailing `client?: PoolClient` parameter, defaulting to the shared pool (`src/shared/db/connection.ts`) when omitted. This applies to `ILeaveRepository.create`/`findById`/`findByQuery`/`findByReversesRequestId`, `IBalanceRepository.findByKey`/`update`, `IAuditRepository.create`, `INotificationRepository.create`. Repositories never open BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK.
- The calling service owns the unit of work: `LeaveService.cancel` calls `this.uow.withTransaction(async (client) => { ... })`; `PgUnitOfWork` acquires a `PoolClient` from the shared pool, issues BEGIN, runs the callback, COMMITs on success / ROLLBACKs on throw, and always releases the client.
- Inside the callback the same `client` is threaded to every participating call in order: `balanceRepository.findByKey(..., client, true)` (row lock) → `balanceRepository.update(..., client)` (the single release) → `repository.create(reversal, client)` → `auditService.record(..., client)` → `notificationService.create(..., client)`. `IAuditService.record` and `INotificationService.create` accept and forward the optional trailing `PoolClient` for exactly this reason.
- The pre-transaction reads (`repository.findById`, `assertCanCancel`, the timing guard, `findByReversesRequestId`) happen outside the transaction; the authoritative re-check of "already reversed" is the unique index inside the transaction, so a lost race rolls the whole unit back and no balance is released.
- Read-only paths (`list`, `getById`) open no transaction and forward no client.
